How everything is mute and without understanding that is spoken of God without knowledge of the signature; and how in the human mind the signature lies according to the essence of all essences.

All that is spoken, written, or taught concerning God <gloss>therein being</gloss> without the knowledge of the **signature** <term>Signatur: Böhme’s central concept that the inner, spiritual character of a thing is "signed" or revealed in its outward form</term>, that is <gloss>all</gloss> mute and without understanding; for it comes only <gloss>by</gloss> from a historical delusion <note>original: "historischen wahn" – Böhme uses this to describe knowledge gained only through books or second-hand accounts rather than through direct spiritual experience</note>, <gloss>ay</gloss> from the mouth of another, wherein the spirit is mute without knowledge. But if the spirit opens the signature <gloss>to him</gloss> to him, then he understands the other's mouth and further understands how the spirit has revealed itself from the **essence** <term>Essentz: the fundamental spiritual substance or "being" of a thing</term> through the **principle** <term>Principium: a foundational source or beginning point in Böhme's cosmology</term> in sound with the voice.

<summary>Böhme introduces the "Signature," arguing that theological knowledge is mere "historical delusion" unless one understands the spiritual language revealed in the forms of things. He uses the metaphor of a hammer striking a bell to describe how one person's spirit must resonate with another's for true understanding to occur.</summary>

we recognize that all human attributes come from one, <gloss>and</gloss> that they have only one single root and mother; otherwise, one human could not understand another in sound. For with the sound or speech, the form imprints itself into another's **likeness** <note>original: "Gestaltnuß" — referring to the inner configuration or spiritual image of a person</note>; a similar sound catches and moves the other. And in the sound, the spirit imprints its own likeness (which it has drawn <gloss>out of the material</gloss> **essence** <term>Essentz: the fundamental spiritual substance of a thing</term> and has brought it into form in the **Beginning** <term>Principio: the foundational source or starting point in Böhme's cosmology</term>).

So that one can understand in the word what the spirit has created for itself, whether in evil or good; and with the same imprint, it enters into another person's likeness and awakens such a form in the **signature** <term>Signatur: the outward manifestation of an inner, spiritual reality</term> within them as well, so that both their likenesses **co-qualify** <term>inqualiren: Böhme’s term for how different qualities or spirits interact, blend, and work within one another</term> with each other in one form; then it is one conception, one will, one spirit, and also one understanding.

# CHAPTER VIII.

->On the Sulphurous Seething <note>original: "Sulphurischen Sude." The reader should now consider that which was written previously regarding the <term>Center of the Birth</term> <note>Centro der Gebährung: the divine point of origin from which all life and matter radiate into existence</note> of all beings; thus he can easily proceed here. <summary>Böhme describes Christ's temptation as an alchemical transmutation where the "fiery" wrath of the soul is transformed into the "light" of divine love. He uses the figure of Mercury to explain how the active spirit of humanity was surrendered back to God's creative Word.</summary>

By the image of *John* and *Christ’s* Mother, he should know that the Kingdom of God and the kingdom of this world are two distinct things in his work, and that the Kingdom of God lies enclosed within the Mother—as if within his own work. He must care for this and be its servant, not a master of the Mother, but rather an almsgiver; he must not be a treasure-hoarder or a greedy person. No one shall attain this, nor understand our meaning, who is not willing to be a caretaker of the Mother. The Most High has placed a lock before the understanding of folly, so that it remains blind until it grows weary of searching; this I say with the foundation of truth.

<note>The vocabulary section below defines the technical terms used by Böhme on this page.</note>

*   **Mystery:** Hidden spiritual essence.
*   **Selfhood:** The ego or "I-ness."
*   **Signature:** The outward sign of inner spirit.
*   **Mirror:** Divine reflection in the soul.
*   **Resignation:** Total surrender to God.
*   **Philosophical work:** Alchemy/Spiritual transformation.
*   **Sulfur, Mercury, Salt:** The three essential chemical/spiritual principles.
*   **Sun:** The source of light and life in the physical world.
*   **Impression:** The contracting force of the dark world.
*   **Universal:** The restored, divine whole.

# CONCERNING THE SIGNATURE
<note>original: *DE SIGNATVRA*</note>

...of the disgust <note>original: *Eckel*; in Böhme's thought, this is the soul's profound revulsion toward its own sinful, selfish nature</note> against God. Whoever entirely abandons his <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: *selbstheit*; the state of being driven by the individual ego rather than the divine will</note> and gives himself over—with mind and desire, senses and will—into God’s mercy, into the death of **Jesus** Christ, he has died to the earthly world in his will and is a twofold human being. In this state, the disgust works only within itself toward death, <margin>cr</margin> but the <term>resigned will</term> <note>original: *gelassene wille*; the spirit of "Gelassenheit" or yieldedness, where the human will aligns with the divine</note> lives in Christ’s death and <margin>z</margin> continually rises in God through Christ’s resurrection. And though the own-desire <note>The selfish, individualistic craving of the "I"</note> sins—which indeed can do nothing else but sin—nevertheless the resigned <margin>=</margin> will does not live in sin. For it has died to the desire of sin and lives through Christ in God, in the Land of the Living; but the selfhood lives in the Land of Death, as an eternal dying in constant enmity against God.

The earthly human is under God’s curse and is a loathing before God’s holiness; he can seek nothing other than his selfhood, for he is in the <term>wrath</term> <note>original: *Grimm*; the "dark fire" or harsh quality of divine nature that consumes what is not in harmony with love</note> of God. And if he does anything good, he does it not of his own self-will, but rather the will resigned in God forces him so that he must do what he himself does not like to do. And when he does it, he does it only as an <term>instrument</term> <note>original: *werckzeug*</note> of the resigned will—not out of his own desire, but out of God’s will, which guides the resigned will within his desire as a tool.

Therefore, whoever now wishes to behold the Kingdom of God and reach it must lead his soul out of <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: *selbstheit*; the state of being centered on one's own ego and desires</note>, out of the earthly desire, just as a physician leads the cure of a disease out of its painful longing <note>original: *peinliche begierde*; in Böhme’s thought, this refers to the "anguish" or "torment" of the lower nature</note> and leads it into a lovely desire. In this way, the cure of the disease in the body also leads out of the painful longing and into a lovely desire: the disease becomes the servant of the medicine. Likewise, the earthly evil will—when the soul's will is cured—becomes the servant of the <term>resigned will</term> <note>original: *gelassene wille*; the human will that has yielded entirely to the divine</note>.

The <term>elementary and sidereal man</term> <note>The physical body (made of the four elements) and the astral or psychological body (influenced by the "stars" or "sidereal" forces)</note> should only be the tool with which the soul-man works in the resigned will. For God created him for that very purpose; but in **Adam**, the soul made him the master and installed him, and entered into his prison and surrendered its will into it. However, if the soul is to be recognized as God’s child, it must die away from that state again. It must die completely to the earthly selfhood and desire within the Will of God, through the death of **Christ**, and be born entirely anew in God’s will. It must take the power away from the earthly will in its selfhood, and rule over it and hold it in restraint, just as a master guides his tool. Then, selfhood loses its power and <insert>but</insert> gives up the pleasure of selfhood.

<summary>Böhme uses a medical analogy to explain how the soul must reclaim its role as the master over the physical body and the astral mind. He argues that spiritual rebirth requires the ego-driven "selfhood" to become a servant to the divine "resigned will."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the thematic summary of Jacob Böhme’s theosophical concepts, focusing on the relationship between the divine and the human, the alchemical "Three Principles" (Tria Prima), and the necessity of internal spiritual rebirth over external religious observance.</meta>

Divinity and humanity are placed very much over against each other, but not at all in opposition to each other. p. 237.
<note>original Latin: "Ergo non sunt sibi contraria nec separata sed conjuncta, hinc ortâ tentatio Christi. Ejque passio et mors."</note> Therefore they are not contrary to each other nor separate but joined; from this arose the temptation of Christ, and his passion and death.

The element of all being divides itself into four
outer elements. p. 295.

The seven forms of nature make a threefold
spirit: <note>original Latin: "vitam vegetativam sensitivam et animal. seu rationalem"</note> the vegetative, sensitive, and animal or rational life. ibid.

All life consists in Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.
Sulfur is a mother of all spiritual and
physical life. Mercury is the driving force within it, and
Salt is the house or object. p. 296.
<note>In theosophy and alchemy, these "Three Principles" represent the fundamental forces of the universe: Salt (contractive/body), Sulfur (expansive/soul), and Mercury (the mediating flow/spirit).</note>

From the Will arises evil and good, and it can
make the best out of the worst. p. 297.

Of smell, <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "v'stand" (Verstand)</note>, and of taste. p. 336.
> <note>original Latin: "sic preces sunt suavis odor in aspectu Dei. Act. 10."</note> Thus prayers are a sweet odor in the sight of God. Acts 10.

The light of the sun is enclosed in the enclosure <note>original: "claßur," referring to a sealed vessel or a spiritual boundary</note> p. 338.
All creatures turn toward it.

Inner and outer movement of all
creatures. p. 324.

Redemption follows upon the Will
of the soul, since both <term>principles</term> <note>In Böhme's thought, these are the "dark world" of God's wrath and the "light world" of God's love.</note>
are recognized within man. p. 365.
Whichever way he turns, there the
choice is confirmed and established.

Whoever stands only in the outer form of Christianity
but does not give birth to Christ <note>A reference to the mystical concept of "Christ's birth in the soul."</note>, they are no
Christian, nor a true teacher
of Christ. For the form breaks, but the
spirit remains free. p. 376.
